summary: Canfor's 1948 tower on Lookout Mountain; removed from the fire system in 1987 and replaced by a replica in 2013-2014.

facts.design: Replica tower in modern construction; the 1950 original was a pre-fabricated hip-roof cabin with cupola
facts.status_note: The 1950 lookout was dismantled and a replica tower stands on the site.

staffing.status: appointed lookoutman during fire season until removal from the fire protection system

access.note: Day-use recreation site. A steep access trail leads from a trailhead and parking area that the replica project improved.

visit.trail_note: Steep trail; allow about 4 hours round trip. Day use only. Campfires prohibited.

events.note: Canfor built a 6.1 to 7.6 m (20 to 25 ft) tower with a plywood cupola, a tent and an access trail.
A BC Forest Service lookoutman was stationed at the lookout.
BC Forest Service took the site over from Canfor.
Tent and tower replaced by a permanent pre-fabricated hip-roof cabin with cupola.
Kay fire burned the area east and south of the lookout; the building was not damaged.
A new metal roof was installed.
Deleted from the provincial fire protection system. The brochure says it then fell into disrepair.
Woss Residents' Association proposed rehabilitating the lookout and building an access trail.
Brochure dates the removal of the 1950 structure to 2013-2014.
Replica tower built through combined efforts of volunteers, agencies and organizations. A tourism page gives 2014; the brochure gives 2013-2014.

notes_for_editor: Brief lists status standing and access unknown. The standing structure is a 2013-2014 replica, not the 1950 original; story says so. Access level public is from the day-use description on the tourism page; a search snippet says the lookout is shuttered for winter and reopens in May, but no fetched page confirms it, so it is left out. The Island Coastal Economic Trust project record lists a Year Approved of 2016, which does not match the 2013-2014 and 2014 construction dates; the quote for that year could not be cited cleanly, so the story omits it. No current height is given in any source. Brief design, height and status are not wrong but are incomplete. The brochure's 2,080 ft summit figure does not convert exactly from 640 m (about 2,100 ft); the story keeps the printed figure. Verification 2026-10-20: all 36 quotes found on the first run; story wording tightened where it copied quotes, the helicopter pad purpose and 2013-2014 date range corrected to the sources.
